extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, applicants, and inventors seeking U.S. software-related patent protection (post-Alice)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for drafting and prosecuting U.S. software-related utility patent applications to survive 35 U.S.C. §101/Alice challenges and improve allowance/retention rates. Focuses on claim content, prosecution strategies, and complementary protections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions that do something
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim software that causes something tangible to happen, as opposed to evaluating or organizing something that already exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wherever possible, claim software that causes hardware/computer operation improvements (e.g., improvements to the processor, memory, displays, etc.). Avoid describing or claiming post-solution activity such as displaying, reporting, or printing. Focus patenting resources on software that effects a change rather than merely processes information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer-technology-specific claiming
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft claims that are necessarily rooted in computer technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, draft claims tied to computer/website/technology specifics so that the invention is technically grounded rather than framed as an abstract idea implemented on a generic computer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Group 3600 (and other high-101 groups)
rubrics_metrics.description: Craft claims to avoid USPTO examining groups with high 101 rejection rates (notably groups 3600 and 3700).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claim drafting and filing strategies (e.g., claim phrasing, choice of claim focus) that route examination to art units/examining groups less prone to §101 rejections. Be aware that allowance rates and rejection tendencies vary by art unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name the specific technical benefit and define the problem solved
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor the application and claims to a specific technical benefit afforded by the claimed invention and include a clear definition of the problem solved and the specific technical solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give concrete technical benefits (examples in the article: faster search times within a database, smaller memory requirements for a database, more dynamic or efficient information filtering, more accurate image-sound synchronization, producing more realistic expressions or movement in animated characters). Do not merely argue that the computer generally improves an existing system; instead, teach how the claimed invention improves the existing technology and include precise language delimiting the type of data and how it is handled (see Core Wireless example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain how the invention is not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively rebut the 'abstract idea' prong of the Alice analysis by showing the claims are directed to an improvement in computer functionality or are otherwise non-abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Federal Circuit precedents (e.g., Enfish v. Microsoft) and their progeny to support arguments that software claims are not inherently abstract and can be analyzed under step one of Alice. Ask whether the claims are directed to an improvement to computer functionality and frame the disclosure and claims accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include more independent claims of varying scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider claiming the invention with additional independent claims that vary in scope and language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include broader and narrower independent claims, and consider using 'means for' language where helpful to avoid functional claiming traps. Varying claim scope can help identify allowable claim sets and provide fallback positions during prosecution or in continuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recite the improvement steps in the claim language
rubrics_metrics.description: Recite the specific steps or rules that produce the claimed improvement directly in the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO and courts have pointed to cases (e.g., McRO, Finjan) where claims survived §101 review because they recited concrete steps/rules for improving computer functionality (e.g., rules for animation lip-sync or steps to generate and link a security profile). Draft claims to include those implementation steps rather than high-level outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examiner interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Interview the examiner to discuss technical details and 101 rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews help build rapport, allow practitioners/inventors to describe technical details (often without making limiting file history statements), and may reveal the examiner's view on §101/Alice. Because application of §101 can vary between art units and examiners, interviews can clarify issues and identify paths to allowance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appeals strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner is entrenched on a §101 rejection but you have good arguments, consider prosecuting other rejections first and then appealing on the §101 grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overcome rejections under §§112, 102, 103 where feasible and then file an appeal on the §101 rejection; fresh panels or different adjudicators (PTAB, Federal Circuit) may view the §101 issues differently and yield successful outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use continuations to refine claims over time
rubrics_metrics.description: If needed, narrow claims to overcome a §101 rejection and file continuation applications to pursue alternative claim scopes later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuations allow you to preserve multiple claim strategies while awaiting additional guidance from PTAB, Federal Circuit, or the Supreme Court. As new case law or PTAB decisions issue, continuation prosecution can be shaped to avoid §101 rejections based on evolving precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build layered and diverse protections around software inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider complementary IP protections in addition to utility patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use copyright and trade secret protections and consider design patents to protect user-interface/appearance aspects (look of a computer monitor, handheld device display, computer-generated icons, fonts) under 35 U.S.C. §171. Layered protection can mitigate the risk if utility patent protection is narrowed or lost under §101.
